scenario: WIBTA if I told my cousin his kid can’t stay in our house? | My cousin (M27) recently moved in with my husband and I. We completely closed of the very large main bedroom and bathroom to create a flatlet for him that’s separate from the house with his own entrance so it’s basically two separate units of one house. Now my cousin has a 2 year old and he’s busy with a custody battle with his ex so he can get to spend more time with his son. I completely support this and really hopes he gets more time with his son. Yesterday my cousin came to ask me if it would be possible for my husband and I to convert our spare bedroom into a room for his son if and when he comes to visit over weekends. There is no access from my cousin’s room into our part of the house and he doesn’t have keys to come and go as he pleases. I understand that the court will be looking into his living situation to see if he has suitable space for his son to stay with him (and to be honest his current room and bathroom is more than big enough) but I’m not comfortable with letting his son sleep in our house if my cousin has no access to him and I’m not willing to take responsibility for his kid. The whole family is involved in this because that’s just the way my family is and everyone expects me to help out my cousin with his current custody situation to get him more time with his son. WIBTA for telling him I will not allow his son to sleep in our house and completely jeopardizing his court case?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether it's right or wrong for me to tell my cousin that his kid can't stay in our house. Let me break this down step by step. First, my cousin moved in with my husband and me. We converted the main bedroom and bathroom into a separate flatlet for him, so he has his own entrance and it's pretty much two separate units under one roof. That seems like a good arrangement because it gives him privacy and space. Now, my cousin has a 2-year-old, and he's going through a custody battle with his ex. I completely support him wanting to spend more time with his son. It's important for a child to have a relationship with both parents, especially at such a young age. I really hope he gets more time with his son. Yesterday, he asked if we could convert our spare bedroom into a room for his son. The thing is, there's no access from his flatlet into our part of the house, and he doesn't have keys to come and go as he pleases. So, if his son is staying in our house, he can't just pop in whenever he wants. That makes me uncomfortable because I don't want to be responsible for his kid if something happens and he can't get to his son quickly. I also understand that the court is looking into his living situation to see if he has suitable space for his son. His current flatlet is more than big enough, so I don't think converting our spare room is necessary. Plus, I'm not comfortable letting his son stay in our house without my cousin having easy access. It feels like I'm taking on too much responsibility for his child, and I'm not sure if that's fair to us or to him. The whole family is involved in this because that's just how my family is. Everyone expects me to help out my cousin with his custody situation to get him more time with his son. But I'm not sure if that's the right approach. I want to support him, but I also need to consider our own boundaries and comfort levels. So, the question is: Would it be wrong (WIBTA) for me to tell my cousin I won't allow his son to stay in our house, potentially jeopardizing his court case? I need to think about the implications of both saying yes and no. If I say yes, I'm supporting him, but I'm also putting myself in a situation where I might feel uncomfortable or responsible for his child. If I say no, I'm setting a boundary, but it might affect his custody case and make him spend less time with his son. I also need to consider the legal aspect. The court is evaluating his living situation, so having a separate room might help his case. But if I refuse, it could look like I'm not supporting him, which might not be good for his custody battle. On the other hand, I have to think about my own well-being and the boundaries I've set. It's important to respect my own limits, especially when it comes to taking care of someone else's child. I don't want to end up in a situation where I'm constantly worrying about his son or feel like I'm being taken advantage of. Maybe there's a middle ground. Could we find another solution that supports him without making me uncomfortable? Like, maybe he could stay in a different part of the house or find another arrangement. But given the current setup, it's not possible because the flatlet is already separate. I also wonder if the family's expectation is putting undue pressure on me. It's important to support family, but it's equally important to maintain my own boundaries. I don't want to feel like I'm being forced into something I'm not comfortable with. In the end, I have to weigh the support for my cousin against my own comfort and responsibility. It's a tough spot because I care about him and his son, but I also need to take care of myself and my own home.
